title: Haar Measure and Local Fields
text:
Let \(X\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space, let \(\mathcal B(X)\) denote its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, and let
\[
C_c(X)=\{f:X\to\mathbb R : f \text{ is continuous and compactly supported}\}.
\]



Definition 1.1 (Radon measure) A Radon measure on \(X\) is a positive Borel measure \(\mu\) such that

\(\mu(K)<\infty\) for every compact set \(K\subseteq X\);
\(\mu\) is inner regular on open sets: \[
\mu(U)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq U,\ K\text{ compact}\};
\]
\(\mu\) is outer regular on Borel sets: \[
\mu(E)=\inf\{\mu(U):E\subseteq U,\ U\text{ open}\}.
\]

On a locally compact Hausdorff space, these regularity conditions make integration against \(\mu\) compatible with the topology of \(X\).


Definition 1.2 (Positive linear functional on C_c(X)) A linear map
\[
\Lambda:C_c(X)\longrightarrow \mathbb R
\]
is positive if
\[
f\ge 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Lambda(f)\ge 0.
\]
Positivity already implies the local boundedness needed in the Riesz representation theorem: for every compact \(K\subseteq X\), the restriction of \(\Lambda\) to functions supported in \(K\) is bounded in the uniform norm.


Theorem 1.1 (Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation theorem) The assignment
\[
\mu\longmapsto \Lambda_\mu,
\qquad
\Lambda_\mu(f)=\int_X f(x)\,d\mu(x),
\]
is a bijection between Radon measures on \(X\) and positive linear functionals on \(C_c(X)\).
In particular, every positive linear functional \(\Lambda\) has the form
\[
\Lambda(f)=\int_X f\,d\mu
\]
for a unique Radon measure \(\mu\).

The uniqueness is especially useful for invariant measures: if a positive functional is invariant under a group action on \(C_c(X)\), its representing Radon measure is invariant under the corresponding action on \(X\).



From now on, let \(G\) be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group.

Definition 1.3 (Haar measure) A left Haar measure on \(G\) is a nonzero Radon measure \(\mu_L\) satisfying
\[
\mu_L(gE)=\mu_L(E)
\]
for every \(g\in G\) and every Borel set \(E\subseteq G\).
A right Haar measure on \(G\) is a nonzero Radon measure \(\mu_R\) satisfying
\[
\mu_R(Eg)=\mu_R(E).
\]


Remark 1.1 (The two translation actions on C_c(G)). There are two natural actions of \(G\) on \(C_c(G)\):
\[
(L_gf)(x)=f(g^{-1}x),
\qquad
(R_gf)(x)=f(xg).
\]
A measure \(\mu_L\) is left Haar exactly when
\[
\int_G L_gf\,d\mu_L=\int_G f\,d\mu_L
\]
for all \(g\in G\) and \(f\in C_c(G)\). The analogous statement with \(R_g\) characterizes right Haar measure.


Theorem 1.2 (Haar-Weil theorem: existence) Every locally compact Hausdorff group admits a left Haar measure and a right Haar measure.

The theorem is often proved by first constructing a nonzero positive translation-invariant functional on \(C_c(G)\) and then applying Theorem 1.1.


For a function \(f\in C_c(G)\) and a Borel set \(E\subseteq G\), set
\[
\check f(g)=f(g^{-1}),
\qquad
E^{-1}=\{g^{-1}:g\in E\}.
\]
If \(\mu\) is right Haar, define
\[
\check\mu(E)=\mu(E^{-1}).
\]
Then \(\check\mu\) is left Haar. Conversely, inversion sends left Haar measure to right Haar measure. In integral form,
\[
\int_G f(g)\,d\check\mu(g)
=
\int_G \check f(g)\,d\mu(g)
=
\int_G f(g^{-1})\,d\mu(g).
\]





Theorem 1.3 (Uniqueness of Haar measure) Any two left Haar measures on \(G\) differ by multiplication by a positive scalar. The same is true of right Haar measures.

Fix a right Haar measure \(\mu\) on \(G\), and let
\[
\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{cts}}(G)
\]
be the group of continuous automorphisms of \(G\).

Proposition 1.1 (Modulus of an automorphism) For each \(u\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{cts}}(G)\), there is a unique number \(\delta(u)>0\) such that
\[
\mu(u(E))=\delta(u)\mu(E)
\]
for every Borel set \(E\subseteq G\).
The number \(\delta(u)\) is independent of the chosen right Haar measure, and
\[
\delta:\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{cts}}(G)\longrightarrow\mathbb R_{>0}
\]
is a group homomorphism. Equipped with the Braconnier topology, \(\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{cts}}(G)\) is a topological group and \(\delta\) is continuous. Thus
\[
\delta(u_1u_2)=\delta(u_1)\delta(u_2).
\]
Equivalently, for every \(f\in C_c(G)\),
\[
\int_G f(u(x))\,d\mu(x)
=
\delta(u)^{-1}\int_G f(x)\,d\mu(x).
\]

Indeed, the measure \(E\mapsto\mu(u(E))\) is again right Haar, so Theorem 1.3 supplies the scalar. Replacing \(\mu\) by \(c\mu\) does not change that scalar, and composition of automorphisms proves multiplicativity.

Definition 1.4 (Modular character) The conjugation map is
\[
\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{Inn}(G)
\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{cts}}(G),
\qquad
\operatorname{Ad}(g)(x)=gxg^{-1}.
\]
The modular character of \(G\) is
\[
\delta_G:G\longrightarrow\mathbb R_{>0},
\qquad
\delta_G(g)=\delta(\operatorname{Ad}(g)).
\]

This convention is tied to the fixed right Haar measure: \(\mu(gE)=\delta_G(g)\mu(E)\). Authors who begin with a left Haar measure sometimes use the reciprocal function, so the defining change-of-variables identity should always be checked.


Let \(E\in\mathcal B(G)\) and \(g\in G\). Since \(\mu\) is right invariant,
\[
\mu(gE)
=
\mu(gEg^{-1})
=
\delta_G(g)\mu(E).
\]
Likewise, for \(f\in C_c(G)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_G f(gx)\,d\mu(x)
&=\int_G f(gxg^{-1})\,d\mu(x)\\
&=\delta_G(g)^{-1}\int_G f(x)\,d\mu(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses right invariance, while the second is the change-of-variables formula for \(\operatorname{Ad}(g)\).





Definition 1.5 (Unimodular group) The group \(G\) is unimodular if
\[
\delta_G\equiv 1.
\]
Equivalently, every right Haar measure is also left Haar.


Example 1.1 (Basic unimodular groups) Each of the following is unimodular:

every abelian locally compact group, because every inner automorphism is the identity;
every compact group, because the image of the continuous homomorphism \(\delta_G:G\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) is compact, and the only compact subgroup of \(\mathbb R_{>0}\) is \(\{1\}\);
every discrete group, because counting measure is both left and right invariant.



Example 1.2 (Lebesgue measure on R^n) The additive group \(\mathbb R^n\) is unimodular. Its automorphism group is \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb R)\), and Lebesgue measure satisfies
\[
\delta_{\mathbb R^n}(A)=|\det A|,
\qquad A\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb R).
\]
Here \(\delta_{\mathbb R^n}(A)\) is the automorphism modulus from Proposition 1.1, not the modular character of the abelian group \(\mathbb R^n\).


Example 1.3 (Haar measure on R^times) The measure
\[
d^\times x=\frac{dx}{|x|}
\]
is Haar measure on the multiplicative group \(\mathbb R^\times\). Indeed, the substitution \(x=ay\) gives
\[
\frac{dx}{|x|}=\frac{|a|\,dy}{|a||y|}=\frac{dy}{|y|}.
\]


Example 1.4 (The upper-triangular subgroup) Let
\[
B=
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b\\
0&c
\end{pmatrix}
:a,c\in\mathbb R^\times,\ b\in\mathbb R
\right\}
\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R).
\]
Then
\[
\delta_B\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b\\
0&c
\end{pmatrix}
\right)
=
\left|\frac{a}{c}\right|.
\]
The same formula holds over an arbitrary local field after replacing the ordinary absolute value by the normalized absolute value of that field. A direct calculation appears at the end of the note.

section: 2.1 The normalized absolute value from Haar measure
text:
2.1 The normalized absolute value from Haar measure
For \(a\in F^\times\), multiplication by \(a\) is a continuous automorphism
\[
m_a:(F,+)\longrightarrow(F,+),
\qquad
x\longmapsto ax.
\]

Definition 2.1 (Module of multiplication) Define
\[
\lVert a\rVert_F=\delta_{(F,+)}(m_a)>0
\qquad(a\in F^\times),
\]
and set \(\lVert0\rVert_F=0\). We call \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_F\) the Haar-normalized absolute value, or module, of \(F\).
By construction,
\[
\lVert ab\rVert_F=\lVert a\rVert_F\lVert b\rVert_F.
\]

If \(\mu_F\) is additive Haar measure, the defining change-of-variables identities are
\[
\mu_F(aE)=\lVert a\rVert_F\mu_F(E)
\]
and
\[
\int_F f(ax)\,d\mu_F(x)
=
\lVert a\rVert_F^{-1}\int_F f(x)\,d\mu_F(x).
\]

Proposition 2.1 (Associated ordinary absolute value) With the standard local-field normalization, there is a number \(t_F>0\) such that
\[
|x|=\lVert x\rVert_F^{1/t_F}
\]
is an ordinary absolute value inducing the original topology on \(F\). In the classification below,
\[
t_F=
\begin{cases}
2,&F\cong\mathbb C,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the exceptional case is
\[
\lVert z\rVert_{\mathbb C}=z\overline z=|z|^2.
\]


Remark 2.1 (A normalization point). Without fixing a convention, the exponent in Proposition 2.1 is not unique: positive powers can define equivalent absolute values. The values of \(t_F\) above are the standard choices compatible with Haar measure and the usual absolute value on \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb C\); in the nonarchimedean case, the module \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_F\) itself is used.

The metric
\[
d(x,y)=|x-y|
\]
induces the original topology of \(F\). We exclude the discrete topology; in the discrete case the corresponding module is trivial:
\[
\lVert x\rVert_F=
\begin{cases}
1,&x\ne0,\\
0,&x=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Definition 2.2 (Local field of characteristic zero) A local field of characteristic zero is a nondiscrete, locally compact Hausdorff topological field \(F\) with \(\operatorname{char}F=0\).

title: Haar Measure and Local Fields
text:
2.2 Classification of characteristic-zero local fields
The prime field gives an embedding
\[
\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow F.
\]
The restriction of \(|\cdot|\) to \(\mathbb Q\) is nontrivial. Indeed, choose a compact neighborhood \(K\) of \(0\) and a radius \(r>0\) such that \(\overline B(0,r)\subseteq K\). Using nondiscreteness, choose \(x\ne0\) with \(|x|<r\). If \(|n|=1\) for every nonzero \(n\in\mathbb Z\), then all points \(nx\) lie in the compact set \(\overline B(0,r)\) and
\[
|nx-mx|=|n-m|\,|x|=|x|
\]
whenever \(n\ne m\). This would give an infinite \(|x|\)-separated subset of a compact metric space, which is impossible.
Restricting the associated absolute value to \(\mathbb Q\) and applying Ostrowski’s theorem now shows that exactly one of the following occurs:
\[
|\cdot|\big|_{\mathbb Q}
\sim
|\cdot|_\infty
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
|\cdot|\big|_{\mathbb Q}
\sim
|\cdot|_p
\]
for a unique prime \(p\). Here \(\sim\) means that one absolute value is a positive power of the other; equivalent absolute values determine the same topology.

Proposition 2.2 (Completeness) The field \(F\) is complete for the metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\).

Proof. Translations act transitively on \(F\) by isometries. Choose a compact neighborhood \(K\) of \(0\). Since the metric topology is the given topology, some closed ball \(\overline B(0,r)\) is contained in \(K\) and is therefore compact. Translation then shows that every closed ball
\[
\overline B(x,r)=x+\overline B(0,r)
\]
is compact. If \((x_n)\) is Cauchy, then some tail lies in one such compact ball. That tail has a convergent subsequence, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit. Hence \(F\) is complete. \(\square\)
Consequently, the closure of \(\mathbb Q\) in \(F\) is isomorphic either to \(\mathbb R\) or to \(\mathbb Q_p\). Thus \(F\) is a topological vector space over one of these two complete fields.

Theorem 2.1 (Weil’s finite-dimensionality theorem) Let \(K\) be a nondiscrete locally compact field. If \(V\) is a Hausdorff topological \(K\)-vector space that is locally compact, then
\[
\dim_KV<\infty.
\]

Applying Theorem 2.1 to \(V=F\) gives
\[
[F:\mathbb R]<\infty
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
[F:\mathbb Q_p]<\infty.
\]
We arrive at the classification.

Theorem 2.2 (Classification) Every characteristic-zero local field is isomorphic, as a topological field, to exactly one of the following types:

an archimedean local field, namely \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\);
a nonarchimedean local field, namely a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\) for a unique prime \(p\).


For \(F=\mathbb R\), one has \(t_F=1\). For \(F=\mathbb C\), one has \(t_F=2\) because multiplication by \(z\) on the real vector space \(\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2\) has determinant \(z\overline z\). For a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\), the module \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_F\) is already nonarchimedean, so the standard choice is \(t_F=1\).

title: Haar Measure and Local Fields
section: 3.1 The valuation ring, maximal ideal, and uniformizer
text:
3.1 The valuation ring, maximal ideal, and uniformizer
Define
\[
\mathcal O_F=\{x\in F:|x|_F\le1\},
\qquad
\mathfrak p_F=\{x\in F:|x|_F<1\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal O_F\) is a compact open subring of \(F\), and
\[
\mathcal O_F^\times=\{x\in F:|x|_F=1\}.
\]
The ring \(\mathcal O_F\) is a discrete valuation ring. Its unique maximal ideal is \(\mathfrak p_F\), and there is a uniformizer \(\varpi_F\in\mathfrak p_F\) such that
\[
\mathfrak p_F=\varpi_F\mathcal O_F.
\]
Every \(x\in F^\times\) admits a unique decomposition
\[
x=\varpi_F^{v_F(x)}u,
\qquad
v_F(x)\in\mathbb Z,
\quad
u\in\mathcal O_F^\times.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
F^\times=\varpi_F^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathcal O_F^\times,
\]
and the normalized valuation
\[
v_F:F^\times\longrightarrow\mathbb Z
\]
is characterized by \(v_F(\varpi_F)=1\).
The residue field
\[
k_F=\mathcal O_F/\mathfrak p_F
\]
is finite. Put
\[
q=\#k_F.
\]
Because \([\mathcal O_F:\mathfrak p_F]=q\), additive Haar measure normalized by \(\mu_F(\mathcal O_F)=1\) satisfies
\[
\mu_F(\mathfrak p_F)=q^{-1}.
\]
It follows that
\[
|x|_F=q^{-v_F(x)}.
\]

title: Haar Measure and Local Fields
text:
3.2 Natural filtrations
The powers of the maximal ideal form a decreasing additive filtration
\[
\mathcal O_F\supset\mathfrak p_F\supset\mathfrak p_F^2\supset\cdots,
\]
and the higher unit groups
\[
U_F^n=1+\mathfrak p_F^n,
\qquad n\ge1,
\]
form a decreasing multiplicative filtration
\[
\mathcal O_F^\times\supset U_F^1\supset U_F^2\supset\cdots.
\]

title: Haar Measure and Local Fields
text:
3.3 Hensel’s lemma

Lemma 3.1 (Hensel’s lemma: factorization form) Let \(P\in\mathcal O_F[X]\) be monic. Suppose that its reduction modulo \(\mathfrak p_F\) factors as
\[
\overline P=\overline A\,\overline B
\qquad\text{in }k_F[X],
\]
where \(\overline A\) and \(\overline B\) are monic and relatively prime. Then there are unique monic polynomials \(A,B\in\mathcal O_F[X]\) satisfying
\[
A\bmod\mathfrak p_F=\overline A,
\qquad
B\bmod\mathfrak p_F=\overline B,
\qquad
P=AB.
\]


Corollary 3.1 (Simple roots lift) Let \(P\in\mathcal O_F[X]\). If \(\overline a\in k_F\) is a simple root of \(\overline P\), then there is a unique \(a\in\mathcal O_F\) reducing to \(\overline a\) such that
\[
P(a)=0.
\]

Apply Corollary 3.1 to \(P(X)=X^{q-1}-1\). Since \(p\nmid q-1\), every nonzero residue class is a simple root. Therefore reduction induces an isomorphism
\[
\mu_{q-1}(F)\xrightarrow{\sim}k_F^\times,
\]
where
\[
\mu_{q-1}(F)=\{x\in F^\times:x^{q-1}=1\}.
\]
The exact sequence
\[
1\longrightarrow U_F^1
\longrightarrow\mathcal O_F^\times
\longrightarrow k_F^\times
\longrightarrow1
\]
therefore splits via the Teichmuller representatives \(\mu_{q-1}(F)\). Hence
\[
\mathcal O_F^\times
\cong
\mu_{q-1}(F)\times U_F^1
\cong
k_F^\times\times U_F^1.
\]

Example 3.1 (Prime-to-p roots of unity) For \(x\in F^\times\),
\[
x\in\mu_{q-1}(F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\text{ has finite order relatively prime to }p.
\]
Indeed, reduction is injective on prime-to-\(p\) torsion, while \(k_F^\times\) is cyclic of order \(q-1\).

title: Definitions
text:
Equivalent definitions

Definition 1 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is étale if it is

locally of finite presentation,
flat, and
unramified.



Definition 2 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between nonsingular varieties over \(k\) is étale if it induces isomorphisms on the tangent spaces at all points of \(X\).


Definition 3 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is étale if it is smooth of relative dimension \(0\).


Remark 1. The second definition tells us that we can think of an étale map as a map that is locally an isomorphism. And for the definitions of the flat, unramified and smooth morphisms, see later.

title: Definitions
text:
Examples

Example 1 (open immersion) Every open immersion \(U\hookrightarrow X\) is étale. Nothing changes near a point of \(U\): we have only restricted our attention to a smaller open subset.


Example 2 Assume that \(n\) is invertible in the base field. On the punctured affine line, the map
\[
\mathbb G_m \longrightarrow \mathbb G_m, \qquad t\longmapsto t^n
\]
is étale. Infinitesimally, its derivative is \(nt^{n-1}\), which never vanishes on \(\mathbb G_m\).







WarningWhere the picture breaks



On the whole affine line, \(t\mapsto t^n\) ramifies at \(t=0\). The map is no longer étale there: the branches collide.

title: Smooth Morphisms Again
text:
No global Noetherian hypothesis is needed below; the relevant finiteness assumptions are stated explicitly. For a morphism \(\pi:X\to Y\), write
\[
\Omega_{X/Y}=\Omega^1_{X/Y}
\]
for the sheaf of relative Kähler differentials. If \(y\in Y\), then
\[
X_y := X\times_Y \operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)
\]
denotes the fiber over \(y\). A geometric fiber is the further base change \(X_{\bar y}=X_y\times_{\kappa(y)}\overline{\kappa(y)}\).

Definition 1 Let \(R\) be a ring and let
\[
B=
\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}.
\]
The morphism
\[
\operatorname{Spec}B\longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}R
\]
is standard smooth of relative dimension \(n\) if some \(r\times r\) minor of the Jacobian matrix
\[
J(f)=
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_
{\substack{1\le i\le r\\1\le j\le n+r}}
\]
is invertible in \(B\). After reordering the variables, one may assume that
\[
\det\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\le i,j\le r}
\in B^\times.
\]
A morphism is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) precisely when it is locally, on both source and target, of this form.

For a standard smooth presentation, the conormal sequence is
\[
(f_1,\ldots,f_r)/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)^2
\longrightarrow
\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n+r}B\,dx_j
\longrightarrow
\Omega_{B/R}
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The invertible Jacobian minor allows \(dx_1,\ldots,dx_r\) to be eliminated. Consequently,
\[
\Omega_{B/R}\cong
\bigoplus_{j=r+1}^{n+r}B\,dx_j,
\]
so \(\Omega_{B/R}\) is locally free of rank \(n\).

title: Smooth Morphisms Again
text:
A zero-dimensional smooth immersion

Lemma 1 (Smooth locally closed immersions) Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a locally closed immersion. Then \(f\) is smooth of relative dimension \(0\) if and only if \(f\) is an open immersion.


Proof. Every open immersion is smooth of relative dimension \(0\), so only the converse needs proof.
There is a short conceptual argument. A locally closed immersion is a monomorphism. A smooth morphism of relative dimension \(0\) is étale, and an étale monomorphism is an open immersion.
The following affine calculation records the Jacobian argument behind this fact. Because the assertion is local on \(X\) and \(Y\), shrink around a point of \(X\) so that \(f\) is both a closed immersion and standard smooth of relative dimension \(0\). We may write
\[
X=\operatorname{Spec}B,
\qquad
Y=\operatorname{Spec}R,
\qquad
B=\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_n)},
\]
with
\[
\det J(f)=
\det\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\le i,j\le n}
\in B^\times.
\]
Since \(X\to Y\) is a closed immersion, the ring map \(R\to B\) is surjective. Hence, for every \(i\), there exists \(r_i\in R\) and \(a_{ij}\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) such that
\[
x_i=r_i+\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}f_j.
\]
Differentiate with respect to \(x_\ell\):
\[
\delta_{i\ell}
=
\sum_{j=1}^n
\left(
\frac{\partial a_{ij}}{\partial x_\ell}f_j
+a_{ij}\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_\ell}
\right).
\]
Modulo \((f_1,\ldots,f_n)\), this becomes the matrix identity
\[
I_n=
(a_{ij})_{i,j}
\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_\ell}\right)_{j,\ell}
\qquad\text{in }M_n(B).
\]
The Jacobian matrix is invertible in \(B\), so \((a_{ij})\) is invertible in \(B\) as well. After possibly shrinking once more, the two ideals agree:
\[
(f_1,\ldots,f_n)
=
(x_1-r_1,\ldots,x_n-r_n).
\]
Therefore
\[
B
\cong
\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}
{(x_1-r_1,\ldots,x_n-r_n)}
\cong R.
\]
Thus \(f\) is locally an isomorphism onto an open subscheme of \(Y\). Hence \(f\) is an open immersion.


Remark 1 (Étale interpretation). The lemma is often summarized as
\[
\text{étale monomorphism}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{open immersion}.
\]
The relative-dimension-zero hypothesis is exactly what turns a smooth morphism into an étale morphism.

title: Smooth Morphisms Again
text:
Equivalent criteria for smoothness

Theorem 1 (Fiberwise and differential criteria) Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism of schemes, and let \(n\ge 0\). The following conditions are equivalent.

\(\pi\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\).
\(\pi\) is locally of finite presentation and flat, its fibers have pure dimension \(n\), and \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is locally free of rank \(n\).
\(\pi\) is locally of finite presentation and flat, and every fiber \(X_y\) is a smooth \(\kappa(y)\)-scheme of pure dimension \(n\).
\(\pi\) is locally of finite presentation and flat, and every geometric fiber \(X_{\bar y}\) is a smooth \(\overline{\kappa(y)}\)-scheme of pure dimension \(n\).



Proof. We follow the chain
\[
(1)\Longrightarrow(2)\Longrightarrow(3)
\Longleftrightarrow(4),
\qquad
(3)\Longrightarrow(1).
\]

Step 1: \((1)\Rightarrow(2)\)
Smooth morphisms are locally of finite presentation and flat. Locally, \(\pi\) has a standard smooth presentation
\[
B=
\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}.
\]
By the Jacobian calculation following Definition 1, \(\Omega_{B/R}\) is free of rank \(n\). Standard smooth morphisms have fibers of pure dimension \(n\), so condition (2) follows.


Step 2: \((2)\Rightarrow(3)\)
Fix \(y\in Y\). Formation of Kähler differentials commutes with base change:
\[
\Omega_{X_y/\kappa(y)}
\cong
\Omega_{X/Y}|_{X_y}.
\]
Thus \(\Omega_{X_y/\kappa(y)}\) is locally free of rank \(n\). Since \(X_y\) is of finite type and pure dimension \(n\), the differential form of the Jacobian criterion shows that \(X_y\) is smooth over \(\kappa(y)\).


Step 3: \((3)\Longleftrightarrow(4)\)
Smoothness and pure relative dimension are preserved by arbitrary base change, so (3) implies (4). Conversely, smoothness descends along the faithfully flat field extension
\[
\kappa(y)\subseteq \overline{\kappa(y)}.
\]
Dimension is unchanged under algebraic field extension. Therefore (4) implies (3).


Step 4: \((3)\Rightarrow(1)\)
Fix \(p\in X\), and put \(q=\pi(p)\). Because \(\pi\) is locally of finite presentation, after shrinking around \(p\) and \(q\) we can write
\[
U=\operatorname{Spec}C
\longrightarrow
V=\operatorname{Spec}B,
\qquad
C=\frac{B[x_1,\ldots,x_N]}{I},
\]
where \(I=(f_1,\ldots,f_s)\) is finitely generated. Passing to the fiber over \(q\) gives
\[
\overline U
=
U\times_V\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)
=
\operatorname{Spec}
\frac{\kappa(q)[x_1,\ldots,x_N]}{\overline I}.
\]
By (3), \(\overline U\) is smooth of dimension \(n\) at \(p\). The Jacobian criterion therefore supplies
\[
r=N-n
\]
elements of \(\overline I\), which we may take to be \(\overline f_1,\ldots,\overline f_r\), such that an \(r\times r\) Jacobian minor is invertible near \(p\). Lift these elements to \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I\), and localize so that the same minor is invertible. Set
\[
R=
\frac{B[x_1,\ldots,x_N]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)},
\qquad
J=I/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subseteq R.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{Spec}R\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) is standard smooth of relative dimension \(n\), while
\[
C\cong R/J.
\]
On the fiber over \(q\), the two schemes agree in a neighborhood of \(p\), so
\[
(J\otimes_B\kappa(q))_p=0.
\]
Here is where flatness is essential. From
\[
0\longrightarrow J\longrightarrow R\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow 0
\]
and the flatness of \(C\) over \(B\), tensoring with \(\kappa(q)\) remains exact on the left. Hence the displayed vanishing is genuine, rather than being obscured by a \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^B(C,\kappa(q))\) term. Equivalently,
\[
J_p=\mathfrak m_qJ_p.
\]
Since \(J_p\) is a finite module over the local ring \(R_p\), Nakayama’s lemma gives \(J_p=0\). After shrinking around \(p\), we have \(J=0\), and hence
\[
U\cong\operatorname{Spec}R
\]
is standard smooth of relative dimension \(n\) over \(V\). As \(p\) was arbitrary, \(\pi\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\).



Remark 2. In a fiber of finite type over a field, closed points are dense. Thus one may also run Step 4 first at closed points of the fibers. The standard smooth locus is open, and a nonempty closed subset of a finite-type fiber contains a closed point; consequently, covering all closed points covers the whole fiber.

title: Smooth Morphisms Again
text:
Formal smoothness

Definition 2 A morphism \(\pi:X\to Y\) is formally smooth if the following lifting property holds. For every affine \(Y\)-scheme \(T\) and every closed subscheme \(T_0\hookrightarrow T\) defined by a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf \(\mathcal J\) with \(\mathcal J^2=0\), the restriction map
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(T,X)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(T_0,X)
\]
is surjective.
Equivalently, every commutative diagram
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
T_0 & \longrightarrow & X\\
\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow\!\pi\\
T & \longrightarrow & Y
\end{array}
\]
admits a dotted lift \(T\to X\).

On affine schemes, with \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}R\) and \(X=\operatorname{Spec}B\), formal smoothness says: for every \(R\)-algebra \(C\), every square-zero ideal \(J\subseteq C\), and every \(R\)-algebra map
\[
B\longrightarrow C/J,
\]
there exists an \(R\)-algebra lift \(B\to C\).

Theorem 2 A morphism \(\pi:X\to Y\) is smooth if and only if it is locally of finite presentation and formally smooth.


Proof. We first verify the lifting property for a standard smooth affine morphism. Let
\[
A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}],
\qquad
I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r),
\qquad
B=A/I,
\]
where an \(r\times r\) Jacobian minor is invertible in \(B\). Let \(C\) be an \(R\)-algebra, let \(J\subseteq C\) satisfy \(J^2=0\), and suppose that we are given
\[
\varphi:B\longrightarrow C/J.
\]
Because \(A\) is a polynomial algebra, choose arbitrary lifts in \(C\) of the images of the variables. They define an \(R\)-algebra map
\[
\psi:A\longrightarrow C
\]
lifting \(A\to B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C/J\). Since \(\psi(I)\subseteq J\) and \(J^2=0\), the restriction of \(\psi\) induces a \(B\)-linear map
\[
\overline\psi:I/I^2\longrightarrow J.
\]
For a standard smooth algebra, the conormal sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow I/I^2
\longrightarrow \Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B
\longrightarrow \Omega_{B/R}
\longrightarrow 0
\]
is split exact. Hence \(\overline\psi\) extends to a \(B\)-linear map
\[
\Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B\longrightarrow J.
\]
By the universal property of Kähler differentials, this extension corresponds to an \(R\)-derivation
\[
\delta:A\longrightarrow J
\]
whose restriction to \(I\) equals \(\psi|_I\). Therefore
\[
\psi-\delta:A\longrightarrow C
\]
vanishes on \(I\), so it factors through \(B=A/I\). The resulting map \(B\to C\) is the desired lift of \(\varphi\). Thus every standard smooth morphism is formally smooth, and therefore every smooth morphism is formally smooth.
Conversely, suppose that \(B\) is a finitely presented, formally smooth \(R\)-algebra. Choose a finite presentation
\[
B=A/I,
\qquad
A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_N].
\]
Apply formal smoothness to the square-zero extension
\[
A/I^2\longrightarrow A/I=B,
\qquad
\ker(A/I^2\to A/I)=I/I^2.
\]
The identity map of \(B\) lifts to an \(R\)-algebra section
\[
B\longrightarrow A/I^2.
\]
This infinitesimal section yields a splitting of the conormal sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow I/I^2
\longrightarrow \Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B
\longrightarrow \Omega_{B/R}
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Because the middle term is finite free, \(\Omega_{B/R}\) is finite projective. More concretely, fix \(p\in\operatorname{Spec}B\). After localizing, choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I\) whose classes form a basis of \(I/I^2\). Nakayama’s lemma shows that these elements generate \(I\) near \(p\). Since the inclusion
\[
I/I^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B
\]
is a split injection, its Jacobian matrix has rank \(r\); after shrinking, some \(r\times r\) minor is invertible. Thus \(B\) has a standard smooth presentation near \(p\). It follows that \(B\) is smooth over \(R\), and the scheme-theoretic statement follows by working affine-locally.


Remark 3. Formal smoothness alone is not equivalent to smoothness. For example,
\[
R[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots]
\]
is formally smooth over \(R\), but it is not finitely presented over \(R\), so its spectrum is not smooth over \(\operatorname{Spec}R\) in the usual scheme-theoretic sense. Thus the precise statement is
\[
\boxed{
\text{smooth}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{locally of finite presentation + formally smooth}
}.
\]

title: Smooth Morphisms Again
Smooth Morphisms
text: A smooth morphism is the relative version of a nonsingular variety. Roughly, its fibers are smooth and fit together uniformly over the base.

title: Smooth Morphisms
text:
Defitions

Definition 1 (standard smooth morphism) The projection
\[
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(R)
\]
is called the standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\) if the determinant of the matrix
\[
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}
\]
is invertible in the ring \(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)\).


Remark 1. The fibers of this morphism are smooth varieties of dimension \(n\) by the Jacobian criterion. The condition on the determinant is a relative version of the Jacobian criterion.


Definition 2 (smooth morphism) A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) if there exist open subsets \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\) and \(\{V_i\}\) of \(Y\) such that \(\{U_i\}\) covers \(X\) and \(f(U_i)\subseteq V_i\) for each \(i\), and the restriction \(f|_{U_i}\colon U_i\to V_i\) is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\).


Remark 2. There are several equivalent variants of the definition of a standard smooth morphism that lead to the same notion of a smooth morphism.

We may allow a morphism which factors as \[
U \hookrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\bigr)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}(R),
\] where the first morphism is an open immersion and the second morphism is standard smooth in the sense above.
We may replace the prescribed square Jacobian matrix by the full Jacobian matrix \[
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_
{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\1\leq j\leq n+r}},
\] and require that some \(r\times r\) minor be invertible.

These variants give the same notion of a smooth morphism. If standard smoothness is defined as 1, we may assume \(\{Y_i\}\) covers \(Y\). One can combine 1 and 2 to weaken the standard smoothness again.


Remark 3. It is easy to show that we may define a smooth morphism by requiring that, for every \(x\in X\), there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) and an open neighborhood \(V\) of \(f(x)\) such that the induced morphism \(f\colon U\to V\) is standard smooth. In this formulation, the full-rank condition may be weakened to the requirement that \(df_1,\ldots,df_r\) be linearly independent in the fibre of \(\Omega_{R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/R}\) at \(x\).

title: Smooth Morphisms
text:
Basic properties

Proposition 1 A \(k\)-scheme is smooth of relative dimension \(d\) over \(k\), if it is of pure dimension \(d\), and there exists a cover by affine open sets \(\operatorname{Spec} k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\) where the Jacobian matrix has corank \(d\) at all points (not just closed points).


Proposition 2 If \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\) are smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively, then the composition \(g\circ f\colon X\to Z\) is also smooth of relative dimension \(n+m\).


Proof. This is a local property, so we can assume that \(f\) and \(g\) are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively. Then, by the chain rule, the corresponding Jacobian matrix of the composition \(g\circ f\) is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of \(f\) and \(g\) on the diagonal. Therefore, the determinant of the corresponding square matrix of \(g\circ f\) is the product of determinants of the square matrices of \(f\) and \(g\), which are both invertible. So \(g\circ f\) is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n+m\).


Relation to differentials
We recall the definition and properties of the sheaf of differentials in The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms. The sheaf of differentials can be used to characterize smooth morphisms and smooth varieties.

Proposition 3 A scheme \(X\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) over \(k\) if and only if the sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(n\) and \(X\) is locally of finite type and of pure dimension \(n\).


Proof. Assume \(X\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\). Then, by the relation between smoothness and regualrness, one can show that \(X\) is reduced. Since \(X\) is locally of finite type, the sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is of finite type. By defineion, \(X\) is locally standard smooth over \(k\) of relative dimension \(n\), we conclude that \(\Omega_{X/k}|_x\) is free of rank \(n\) for all \(x\in X\). Thus, \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(n\). The other two conditions follow immediately from the definition of the smoothness.
Conversely, if \(X\) satisfies the conditions, then since \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is characterized by the cokernel of the Jacobian, the corank of the Jacobian must be \(n\), which implies that \(X\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) by Proposition 1.







CautionCaution



It is not easy to show that a smooth variety is reduced. The proof is not included here, but it can be found in the textbook “The Rising Sea”. And the last statement in the proof above is a corollary of Nakayama’s lemma, which is a fundamental result in alegbraic geometry, and both reducedness, finiteness and the constantness of the dimension of fibre matter. See 14.3.J in “The Rising Sea” for details.



Remark 4. When \(f:X\to Y\) is a smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\), \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is locally free of rank \(n\), since this is naturally true if \(f\) is standard.


Proposition 4 Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) and \(\rho\colon Y\to Z\) be morphisms of schemes. If \(\pi\) and \(\rho\) are smooth, then the transitive exact sequence is also exact on the left, which means that the sequence \[
0\to \pi^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Y}\to 0
\]
is exact.


Proof. This is a local property, so we can assume that \(\pi\) and \(\rho\) are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively. In The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms, we know the module of differentials is the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. The injectivity of the left follows from the fact that the Jacobian matrix of \(\rho\circ \pi\) is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of \(\pi\) and \(\rho\) on the diagonal.

In the following, we will discuss the conormal exact sequence.

Theorem 1 Let \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) be a closed immersion of smooth varieties over a field \(k\), with ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\). Then the conormal sheaf \[
\mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y}:=\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2
\] is locally free, and the conormal sequence is a locally split short exact sequence \[
0\longrightarrow \mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y}
\xrightarrow{\delta}i^*\Omega_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{X/k}
\longrightarrow 0,
\] where \(\delta(\overline f)=df|_X\).
Dualizing gives the normal exact sequence \[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal T_{X/k}
\longrightarrow i^*\mathcal T_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\mathcal N_{X/Y}
\longrightarrow 0,
\] where \(\mathcal N_{X/Y}:=(\mathcal N^\vee_{X/Y})^\vee\).


Proof. Differentials and the conormal sheaf commute with field extension, while exactness and finite local freeness descend under faithfully flat base change. We may therefore assume that \(k\) is algebraically closed.
Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth over \(k\), they are regular, and the closed immersion \(i\) is a regular immersion. Thus \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\) is locally free of rank equal to the codimension of \(X\) in \(Y\).
The conormal sequence is always right exact: \[
\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2
\xrightarrow{\delta}i^*\Omega_{Y/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{X/k}
\longrightarrow 0.
\] Set \(\mathcal K=\ker\delta\). Since \(\mathcal K\) is a subsheaf of the locally free sheaf \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\), we have \[
\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal K)
\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)
\subseteq\operatorname{Ass}(\mathcal O_X).
\] As \(X\) is reduced, its associated points are precisely the generic points of its irreducible components. Moreover, every nonzero coherent sheaf has an associated point. Hence it suffices to show that \(\mathcal K_\eta=0\) at every generic point \(\eta\) of \(X\).
Fix such a point \(\eta\), and work locally where \(X\) and \(Y\) have dimensions \(m\) and \(n\), respectively. Since \(X\) is reduced, \(\mathcal O_{X,\eta}=\kappa(\eta)\) is a field. Taking stalks gives a right-exact sequence of vector spaces \[
(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)_\eta
\xrightarrow{\delta_\eta}(i^*\Omega_{Y/k})_\eta
\longrightarrow(\Omega_{X/k})_\eta
\longrightarrow 0.
\] The dimensions of these three vector spaces are \(n-m\), \(n\), and \(m\), respectively. Right exactness therefore gives \[
\dim_{\kappa(\eta)}\operatorname{im}\delta_\eta=n-m
=\dim_{\kappa(\eta)}(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)_\eta.
\] Thus \(\delta_\eta\) is injective. It follows that \(\mathcal K=0\), proving left exactness.
Since \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free, the resulting short exact sequence splits locally. Dualizing a locally split short exact sequence preserves exactness, giving the normal sequence.


Corollary 1 Let \(Y\) be a smooth variety over a field \(k\), and let \(q\in Y\) be a closed point such that \(\kappa(q)/k\) is separable. Write \(\mathfrak m_q\) for the maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O_{Y,q}\). Then the map \[
\mathfrak m_q/\mathfrak m_q^2
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Omega_{Y/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}\kappa(q),
\qquad
\overline f\longmapsto df\otimes 1,
\] is a canonical isomorphism.


Proof. The extension \(\kappa(q)/k\) is finite separable, so \(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)\) is smooth over \(k\) and \(\Omega_{\kappa(q)/k}=0\). Applying the preceding theorem to the closed immersion \(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)\hookrightarrow Y\) gives \[
0\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_q/\mathfrak m_q^2
\longrightarrow\Omega_{Y/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_Y}\kappa(q)
\longrightarrow\Omega_{\kappa(q)/k}
\longrightarrow 0.
\] The last term vanishes, proving the first assertion.







Note



The separability hypothesis is automatic when \(k\) is perfect, in particular when \(\operatorname{char}k=0\) or \(k\) is finite. And the statement still holds when we do not require the smoothness of \(Y\).

title: Étale Morphisms
text:
In this section, we want to explain the equivalent definitions of étale morphsim.
First, as we all known, etale morphism could be defined by smooth morphism of relative dimension \(0\). Thus, it is easy to find that for any smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\), locally factors as \(U\to \mathbb A^n_V\to V\) where the first one is étale and the second one is the structure morphism.
After we establish the fact that we can characterize smooth morphisms by the sheaf of differentials in Smooth Morphisms Again, we could deduce that étale morphisms are the morphisms that are smooth and unramified. Besides, we also know that we could redefine smooth morphism by requiring flatness, locally finitely presented and \(n\)-dimensional smoothness of the fibres. Due to the fact that \(n=0\) and the criterion for unramifiedness by checking fibres, we could then redefine étale morphism by requiring only flatness, unramifiedness and locally finitely presentedness.
For varieties over an algebraically closed field, we know that unramifiedness of morphisms is equivalent to the everywhere-injectness of morphisms induced between the tangent spaces on closed points; and smoothness on a nonsingular point is equivalent to the injectness of morphism induced between the cotangent spaces. For the respect results, see The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms and Smooth Morphisms Again. Therefore, for nonsingular varieties, etale morphisms are exactly the morphisms inducing bijection between (co)tangent spaces on closed points. (Note that closed points are dense and nsmooth locus is open for varieties.)
For other famous propeties of étale morphisms, from the flatness follows the openness, from the unramifiedness follows the fact that the induced diagonal morphism is an open immersion.

title: Flat Morphisms
text: Here we study the properties of flat morphisms that we will need as background for étale morphisms.

title: Flat Morphisms
text:
Flatness

Definition 1 (flat quasi-coherent sheaf over a base) Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) be a morphism of schemes and let \(\mathcal F\) be a quasi-coherent \(\mathcal O_X\)-module. We say that \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\) at \(x\in X\) if the stalk \(\mathcal F_x\) is flat as an \(\mathcal O_{Y,\pi(x)}\)-module. It is flat over \(Y\) if this holds at every point of \(X\).

On affine opens, this reduces to the familiar algebraic notion: if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\), \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), and \(\mathcal F=\widetilde M\), then flatness is controlled by the \(B\)-module \(M\) coming from \(B\to A\).

Lemma 1 With the notation above, \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\) if and only if \(M\) is flat as a \(B\)-module.


Proof. It is an easy commutative algebra exercise.


Corollary 1 If \(\pi:X\to Y\) is an affine morphism, and \(\mathcal F\) is a quasicoherent sheaf on \(X\), then \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\) if and only if \(\pi_*\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y\).







Warningnonexample



The statement may fail even when \(\pi\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
Consider the composite \[
\pi\colon \mathbb P^1_k\hookrightarrow \mathbb P^1_{k[x]} \to \operatorname{Spec}k[x],
\text{ and set }
\mathcal F=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1_k}(-1).
\] Then \(\mathcal F\) is a line bundle and hence flat over \(\mathbb P^1_{k}\).
On the other hand, the global section of \(\pi_*\mathcal F\) is \(H^0(\mathbf P^1_k,\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k}(-1))=0\), which implies that \(\pi_*\mathcal F\) is not flat.



Definition 2 (flat morphism) A morphism \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is flat at \(x\in X\) if the local ring \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\) is flat over \(\mathcal O_{Y,\pi(x)}\). It is flat if it is flat at every point, i.e. \(\mathcal O_X\) is flat over \(Y\).
Equivalently, by Lemma 1, \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is flat if there exist affine open coverings \(X=\bigcup_i X_i\) and \(Y=\bigcup_i Y_i\) such that \(\pi(X_i)\subseteq Y_i\) for each \(i\), and \(A_i\) is flat over \(B_i\) whenever \(X_i=\operatorname{Spec}A_i\) and \(Y_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i\).


Proposition 1 (flat morphisms form a reasonable class) Flat morphisms satisfy the following properties one expects from a geometric class of morphisms:

isomorphisms and open immersions are flat;
the composite \(\phi\circ\pi\colon X\to Z\) is flat whenever both \(\pi\) and \(\phi\) are flat;
flatness is preserved by base change: if \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is flat and \(\psi\colon Y'\to Y\) is any morphism, then \(X\times_Y Y'\to Y'\) is flat;
flatness is local on both the source and the target.



Proof. The assersions 1 and 4 follow immediately by the definition. Assersion 2,3 follow from the corresponding properties for flat quasicoherent sheaves, see Lemma 2 and Lemma 3.


Lemma 2 Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) be a morphism, and let \(\mathcal F\) be a quasicoherent sheaf on \(X\) that is flat over \(Y\). Let \(\phi\colon Y\to Z\) be a flat morphism. Then \(\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Z\).


Proof. By definition, it suffices to check on stalks.


Lemma 3 Let \(X\to Y\) and \(Y'\to Y\) be morphisms. Let \(\mu\colon X'=X\times_Y Y'\to X\) be the projection, and \(\mathcal F\) a quasicoherent sheaf on \(X\) flat over \(Y\). Then \(\mu^*\mathcal F\) is flat over \(Y'\).


Proof. By definition, it suffices to check on stalks. Let \(x'\in X'\). Assume that \(x'\) maps to \(x\in X\), \(y'\in Y'\) and \(y\in Y\) respectively. Then \(\mathcal O_{X',x'}\cong (\mathcal O_{X,x}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}} \mathcal O_{Y',y'})_{\mathfrak p}\) for some prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\). Then \[
(\mu^*\mathcal F)_{x'}\cong (\mathcal O_{X,x}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}} \mathcal O_{Y',y'})_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X,x}}\mathcal F_x.
\] The rest is a commutative algebra exercise.

::: {prp-flat-exact name=““} Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a flat morphism, then the pullback \[
\pi^*:\operatorname{Qcoh}_Y\to\operatorname{Qcoh}_X
\] is an exact functor. :::

title: Flat Morphisms
text:
Criteria of flatness

Proposition 2 (Tor criterion) A \(B\)-module \(M\) is flat if and only if
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^B(M,N)=0
\]
for every \(B\)-module \(N\).


Proposition 3 (ideal criterion) A \(B\)-module \(M\) is flat if and only if, for every finitely generated ideal \(I\subseteq B\), the natural map
\[
I\otimes_B M\longrightarrow M
\]
is injective. The map sends \(a\otimes m\) to \(am\). Equivalently, we can only check \(N\) for finitely generated ideals of \(B\) in Proposition 2.


Proposition 4 Let \((B,\mathfrak n)\) be a local ring and \(M\) a finitely generated \(B\)-module. If \(\operatorname{Tor}(M,B/\mathfrak n)=0\), then \(M\) is free.


Proposition 5 (local criterion) Let \((B,\mathfrak n)\to (A,\mathfrak m)\) be a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, and \(M\) a finitely generated \(A\) module. Then \(M\) is \(B\)-flat if and only if \(\operatorname {Tor}^B_1(M,B/\mathfrak n)=0\).


Proposition 6 (slicing criterion for flatness on the target) Let \((B,\mathfrak n)\to (A,\mathfrak m)\) be a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, \(M\) a finitely generated \(A\)-module, and \(t\in \mathfrak n\) a non-zerodivisor on \(B\). Then \(M\) is flat over \(B\) if and only if

\(t\) is not a zerodivisor on \(M\), and
\(M/tM\) is flat over \(B/(t)\).



Proposition 7 Suppose \((B,\mathfrak n)\to(A,\mathfrak m)\) is a local morphism of Noetherian local rings, \(M\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-module, and \(t\in\mathfrak m\subset A\) is a non-zerodivisor on \(M/\mathfrak nM\). If \(M\) is flat over \(B\), then \(M/tM\) is flat over \(B\)


Closed immersion is well-behaved under the condition of flatness

Proposition 8 (Pullback of quasicoherent sheaves) Let \(0 \to \mathscr{F}' \to \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{F}'' \to 0\) be a short exact sequence of quasicoherent sheaves on a scheme \(Y\), and \(\mathscr{F}''\) is flat. Let \(\pi\colon X \to Y\) be any morphism of schemes. Then the pulled back sequence \(0 \to \pi^*\mathscr{F}' \to \pi^*\mathscr{F} \to \pi^*\mathscr{F}'' \to 0\) remains exact.


Proposition 10 Let \(f\colon X\to Z\) and \(\beta\colon Y\to Z\) be morphisms of schemes, and let \(i\colon V\hookrightarrow X\) be a closed immersion. Set \[
W=X\times_ZY,\qquad V_Y=V\times_ZY,
\] and denote the induced morphisms by \(\alpha\colon W\to X\) and \(i'\colon V_Y\hookrightarrow W\). If either \(\beta\) or the composite \(V\to X\to Z\) is flat, then there is a canonical isomorphism \[
\alpha^*\mathcal I_{V/X}\cong\mathcal I_{V_Y/W}.
\] Equivalently, the pullback of the ideal sequence of \(V\) remains exact: \[
0\longrightarrow\alpha^*\mathcal I_{V/X}
\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W
\longrightarrow i'_*\mathcal O_{V_Y}
\longrightarrow0.
\]

Proof. Since \(i\) is affine, affine base change gives a canonical isomorphism \[
\alpha^*i_*\mathcal O_V\cong i'_*\mathcal O_{V_Y}.
\] The ideal sequence of the closed immersion \(i\) is \[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal I_{V/X}
\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X
\longrightarrow i_*\mathcal O_V
\longrightarrow0.
\] If \(\beta\) is flat, then its base change \(\alpha\) is flat. Hence \(\alpha^*\) is exact, so pulling back the ideal sequence gives \[
0\longrightarrow\alpha^*\mathcal I_{V/X}
\longrightarrow\alpha^*\mathcal O_X
\longrightarrow\alpha^*i_*\mathcal O_V
\longrightarrow0.
\] Using \(\alpha^*\mathcal O_X\cong\mathcal O_W\) and the affine base-change isomorphism above, this becomes the asserted exact sequence. Now suppose instead that \(V\to Z\) is flat. Then \(i_*\mathcal O_V\) is flat over \(Z\). By Proposition 8, we still have the exact sequence we desire.


Flatness and Smoothness
We will show that smooth morphisms are flat.

Proposition 9 Every smooth morphism of schemes is flat.


Proof. We first treat the case in which the schemes are locally Noetherian. Let \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) be smooth, let \(p\in X\), and put \(q=\pi(p)\). After replacing \(X\) and \(Y\) by suitable affine neighborhoods of \(p\) and \(q\), respectively, we may write \(\pi\) in the form
\[
\operatorname{Spec}\!\left(
B[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)
\right)
\longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}B,
\]
where the Jacobian matrix of \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\) has rank \(r\) at \(p\). Set
\[
S=B[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}],
\qquad
A_k=S/(f_1,\ldots,f_k)
\quad (0\leq k\leq r),
\]
and let \(p_k\in\operatorname{Spec}A_k\) be the image of \(p\). We prove inductively that \((A_k)_{p_k}\) is flat over \(B_q\).
For \(k=0\), the ring \((A_0)_{p_0}=S_{p_0}\) is flat over \(B_q\), since a polynomial algebra is flat over its coefficient ring and localization preserves flatness.
Suppose that \((A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}\) is flat over \(B_q\). Let \(t\) denote the image of \(f_k\) in \((A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}\). Since \(p\) lies on \(V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\), we have \(t\in p_{k-1}(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}\). We claim that \(t\) is a non-zerodivisor on the fiber
\[
C_k
=
(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}/q(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}
\cong
\left(
\kappa(q)[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1})
\right)_{\bar p}.
\]
The first \(k\) rows of the Jacobian matrix have rank \(k\) at \(p\). Consequently, the morphism
\[
\operatorname{Spec}A_{k-1}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}B
\]
is smooth at \(p_{k-1}\), so \(C_k\) is reduced.
Choose variables \(x_{j_1},\ldots,x_{j_k}\) such that
\[
\Delta_k
=
\det\!\left(
\frac{\partial f_a}{\partial x_{j_b}}
\right)_{1\leq a,b\leq k}
\]
is a unit at \(\bar p\). On the localized polynomial ring over \(\kappa(q)\), define a derivation by
\[
D(h)
=
\det
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_{j_1}} & \cdots &
\dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_{j_k}}\\
\vdots & & \vdots\\
\dfrac{\partial f_{k-1}}{\partial x_{j_1}} & \cdots &
\dfrac{\partial f_{k-1}}{\partial x_{j_k}}\\
\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x_{j_1}} & \cdots &
\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x_{j_k}}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For \(a<k\), two rows in the determinant defining \(D(f_a)\) coincide, so \(D(f_a)=0\). Thus \(D\) descends to a derivation of \(C_k\), and \(D(t)=\Delta_k\) is a unit in \(C_k\).
If \(g t=0\) in \(C_k\), then
\[
0=D(gt)=D(g)t+gD(t).
\]
Multiplying by \(g\) and using \(gt=0\) gives \(g^2D(t)=0\). Since \(D(t)\) is a unit, \(g^2=0\); since \(C_k\) is reduced, \(g=0\). Hence \(t\) is a non-zerodivisor on \(C_k\).
We may therefore apply the slicing criterion for flatness on the source to the local morphism
\[
(B_q,qB_q)
\longrightarrow
\bigl((A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}},p_{k-1}(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}\bigr),
\]
with \(M=(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}\). It follows that
\[
(A_k)_{p_k}
\cong
(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}/t(A_{k-1})_{p_{k-1}}
\]
is flat over \(B_q\). Induction gives that \((A_r)_{p_r}=\mathcal O_{X,p}\) is flat over \(B_q=\mathcal O_{Y,q}\). Thus \(\pi\) is flat at \(p\), proving the proposition in the locally Noetherian case.
We now remove the Noetherian hypothesis. Flatness is local on the source and target, so around any \(p\in X\) we may choose a standard smooth presentation
\[
U
=
\operatorname{Spec}\!\left(
\bigl(B[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\bigr)_{\Delta}
\right)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}B,
\]
where, after reordering the variables,
\[
\Delta
=
\det\!\left(
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}
\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}
\]
is invertible on \(U\).
Only finitely many coefficients of \(B\) occur in the polynomials \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\). Introduce an indeterminate \(c^i_{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+r}}\) for each such coefficient and let
\[
P
=
\mathbb Z
\left[
c^i_{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+r}}
\right].
\]
Define universal polynomials
\[
g_i
=
\sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+r}}
c^i_{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+r}}
x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_{n+r}^{a_{n+r}}
\in P[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}],
\]
where each sum is finite, and put
\[
\Delta_0
=
\det\!\left(
\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_j}
\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}.
\]
The morphism
\[
U_0
=
\operatorname{Spec}\!\left(
\bigl(P[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]/(g_1,\ldots,g_r)\bigr)_{\Delta_0}
\right)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}P
\]
is smooth. Since \(P\) is Noetherian, the first part of the proof shows that \(U_0\to\operatorname{Spec}P\) is flat.
There is a ring homomorphism \(P\to B\) sending each universal coefficient \(c^i_{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+r}}\) to the corresponding coefficient of \(f_i\). Under this homomorphism, \(g_i\) maps to \(f_i\) and \(\Delta_0\) maps to \(\Delta\). Hence
\[
U
\cong
U_0\times_{\operatorname{Spec}P}\operatorname{Spec}B.
\]
Thus \(\pi|_U\) is obtained from the flat morphism \(U_0\to\operatorname{Spec}P\) by base change. Since flatness is preserved under base change, \(\pi|_U\) is flat. Such neighborhoods \(U\) cover \(X\), so \(\pi\) is flat.

is smooth. Since \(P\) is Noetherian, the first part of the proof shows that \(U_0\to\operatorname{Spec}P\) is flat.
There is a ring homomorphism \(P\to B\) sending each universal coefficient \(c^i_{a_1,\ldots,a_{n+r}}\) to the corresponding coefficient of \(f_i\). Under this homomorphism, \(g_i\) maps to \(f_i\) and \(\Delta_0\) maps to \(\Delta\). Hence
\[
U
\cong
U_0\times_{\operatorname{Spec}P}\operatorname{Spec}B.
\]
Thus \(\pi|_U\) is obtained from the flat morphism \(U_0\to\operatorname{Spec}P\) by base change. Since flatness is preserved under base change, \(\pi|_U\) is flat. Such neighborhoods \(U\) cover \(X\), so \(\pi\) is flat.

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
section: Definition of the sheaf of differentials
text:
Definition of the sheaf of differentials
For schemes \(X\) over \(Y\), there is a quasicoherent sheaf, \(\Omega_{X/Y}\), on \(X\). We call it the sheaf of differentials.

Definition 1 (sheaf of differentials) The sheaf \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is globally defined as the quotient \(\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\), where the ideal sheaf \(\mathscr I\) is the sheaf of ideals defining the diagonal embedding \(X\to X\times_Y X\). One can check that \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is indeed a sheaf on \(X\). We define a map \(d\colon \mathscr O_X\to \Omega_{X/Y}\) by \(d(f)=\operatorname{pr}_1^*f-\operatorname{pr}_2^*f\) for \(f\in \mathscr O_X\).


Proposition 1 Affine locally, if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), then \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is the sheaf associated to the \(A\)-module \(\Omega_{A/B}\), which is generated by symbols \(da\) for \(a\in A\) subject to the relations:

\(d(a+a')=da+da'\) for all \(a,a'\in A\),
\(d(aa')=a\,da'+a'\,da\) for all \(a,a'\in A\), and
\(db=0\) for all \(b\in B\).



Proof. By definition, \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is the sheaf associated to the \(A\)-module \(I/I^2\), where \(I\) is the kernel of the morphism \(A\otimes_B A\to A\). It is generated by elements of the form \(a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\) for \(a\in A\). One can check that the map \(\Omega_{A/B}\longrightarrow I/I^2\) given by \(da\mapsto a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\) is an isomorphism of \(A\)-modules.


Remark 1 (the universal property). The module \(\Omega_{A/B}\) is universal for \(B\)-derivations from \(A\) to an \(A\)-module \(M\). We skip the proof here, but one can find it in any standard textbook on algebraic geometry.

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text:
Basic properties of \(\Omega_{X/Y}\)
There are two standard exact sequences of sheaves of differentials. The first one is the transitivity sequence: for morphisms \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\), there is an exact sequence \[
f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Y}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The second one is the conormal sequence: for a closed immersion \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) with ideal sheaf \(\mathscr I\), there is an exact sequence \[
\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\longrightarrow i^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow 0.
\]






NoteConormal sheaf



We call \(\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\) the conormal sheaf of \(X\) in \(Y\). It is a vector bundle on \(X\) if \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) is a regular immersion.


The sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is compatible with base change: for a cartesian diagram \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X' & \xrightarrow{\mu} & X \\
\downarrow & {\square}\,& \downarrow \\
Y' & \longrightarrow & Y
\end{array}
\] we have a canonical isomorphism \[
\Omega_{X'/Y'}\cong \mu^*\Omega_{X/Y}.
\]
All these properties can be done by using Proposition 1 and the corresponding properties of \(\Omega_{A/B}\).






TipHint



For the two exact sequences, one can check the right one is indeed the cokernel. For the base change property, one can use the universal property of \(\Omega_{A/B}\).


Here is a property for \(\Omega_{A/B}\). For a localization \(S^{-1}A\) of \(A\), we have a canonical isomorphism \[
\Omega_{S^{-1}A/B}\cong S^{-1}\Omega_{A/B}.
\] One can check this using the universal properties of the module of differentials and localization, or using the explicit description of \(\Omega_{A/B}\) in Proposition 1.
There is a proposition characterizing the sheaf of differntials for the fibre product.

Proposition 2 Let \(\alpha:X\to Z\) and \(\beta:Y\to Z\) be morphisms of schemes, and let \(W=X\times_ZY\), with projections \(p:W\to X\) and \(q:W\to Y\). There is a canonical isomorphism \[
p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\oplus q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Omega_{W/Z},
\] given by the sum of the natural maps on differentials.


Proof. Write \[
u:p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow\Omega_{W/Z},
\qquad
v:q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow\Omega_{W/Z}
\] for the natural maps. By transitivity and base change for differentials, we have an exact sequence \[
p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\xrightarrow{u}\Omega_{W/Z}
\xrightarrow{s}q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow 0,
\] where we identify \(\Omega_{W/X}\cong q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\). Naturality gives \(s\circ v=\operatorname{id}\).
Similarly, the natural quotient map \[
\Omega_{W/Z}\longrightarrow\Omega_{W/Y}
\cong p^*\Omega_{X/Z}
\] is a left inverse to \(u\), so \(u\) is injective. Thus the sequence above is short exact and split by \(v\). Consequently, \[
u\oplus v:
p^*\Omega_{X/Z}\oplus q^*\Omega_{Y/Z}
\xrightarrow{\sim}\Omega_{W/Z}
\] is the desired canonical isomorphism.

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text:
Easy calculations of some \(\Omega_{A/B}\)

A useful lemma

Lemma 1 Let \(B\) be a ring and \(A=B[x_1,x_2, \cdots]/(r_1, r_2, \cdots)\) be the ring over \(B\). Then \(\Omega_{A/B}\) is a free \(A\)-module generated by \(dx_1, dx_2, \cdots\) modulo the relations \(dr_1, dr_2, \cdots\).


Proof. For the convenience of the proof, we assume that \(A=B[x_1, x_2, \cdots]\). The general case can be reduced to this case by using the transitivity sequence. Let \(M=\oplus_i A\,e_i\) be the free \(A\)-module generated by \(e_1, e_2, \cdots\). We define a map \(\phi\colon M\to \Omega_{A/B}\) by sending \(e_i\) to \(dx_i\) in \(\Omega_{A/B}\). One can check that \(\phi\) is surjective. To show that \(\phi\) is injective, we construct an inverse map \(\psi\colon \Omega_{A/B}\to M\). For any \(a\in A\), we can write it as a polynomial in \(x_1, x_2, \cdots,x_n\). We define \(\psi(da)\) to be the formal differential of this polynomial. One can check that \(\psi\) is well-defined and is indeed the inverse of \(\phi\).



Differentials for field extensions

Lemma 2 Let \(L/K\) be a separable field extension. Then \(\Omega_{L/K}=0\).


Proof. For any \(\alpha\in L\), there exists a polynomial \(f\in K[x]\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f'(\alpha)\neq 0\). Then \(f'(\alpha)d\alpha=df(\alpha)=0\), which implies \(d\alpha=0\). Since \(\Omega_{L/K}\) is generated by \(d\alpha\) for \(\alpha\in L\), we have \(\Omega_{L/K}=0\).


Lemma 3 Let \(L/K\) be a purely inseparable field extension. Then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\).


Proof. Assume \(\text{char}(K)=p>0\). By the transitivity sequence and the structure of purely inseparable extensions, we may assume \(L=K[x]/(x^p-a)\) for some \(a\in K\). By Lemma 1, we have \(\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dx/(px^{p-1}\,dx)=L\,dx\neq 0\).


Lemma 4 If \(L/K\) is separably genrated by \(t_1,\cdots,t_n\) over \(K\), then \(\Omega_{L/K}\) is a free \(L\)-module generated by \(dt_1,\cdots, dt_n\).


Proof. By Lemma 1 and localization, we have \[\Omega_{K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)/K}\cong K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_n.\]
By Lemma 2, we have \(\Omega_{L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)}=0\), which implies \(\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dt_1+\cdots+ L\,dt_n\) by the transitivity sequence. It remains to show that \(dt_1,\cdots, dt_n\) are linearly independent over \(L\). We will prove this by showing that there exist \(K\) derivations \(d_i\) such that \(d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\). For any \(i\), we can extend the derivation \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t_i}\) on \(K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\) to a derivation \(d_i\) on \(L\) by using the fact that \(L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\) is separable. To be precise, if \(\alpha\in L\) is algebraic over \(K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\), then there exists a polynomial \(f\in K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)[x]\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f'(\alpha)\neq 0\). We can define \(d_i(\alpha)\) to be the unique solution of the equation \(f'(\alpha)d_i(\alpha)+d_i(f)(\alpha)=0\). One can check that \(d_i\) is indeed a derivation on \(L\) and \(d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\).



Differentials for normalization

Example 1 (differentials for the normalization of a curve with a node) Let \[
A=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^2(x+1)),\quad B=k[t],\quad \operatorname{char} k\neq 2,
\] with \(x\mapsto t^2-1\) and \(y\mapsto t(t^2-1)\). The induced map on differentials is \[
dx\longmapsto 2t\,dt,\qquad
dy\longmapsto (3t^2-1)\,dt.
\] Consequently, \[
\Omega_{B/A}
\cong \frac{k[t]}{(2t,3t^2-1)}\,dt=0,
\] since \(\operatorname{char}k\neq 2\) and \[
1=\frac{3}{2}t(2t)-(3t^2-1).
\] Hence the normalization morphism is unramified everywhere, including at \(t=\pm1\), the two points lying over the node.


Example 2 (differentials for the normalization of a curve with a cusp) Let \[
A=k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3),\qquad B=k[t],
\] with normalization map \(x\mapsto t^2\) and \(y\mapsto t^3\). The induced map on differentials is \[
dx\longmapsto 2t\,dt,\qquad
dy\longmapsto 3t^2\,dt.
\] Therefore \[
\Omega_{B/A}
\cong \frac{k[t]}{(2t,3t^2)}\,dt
\cong
\begin{cases}
(k[t]/(t))\,dt, & \operatorname{char}k\neq 2,\\
(k[t]/(t^2))\,dt, & \operatorname{char}k=2.
\end{cases}
\] Thus the normalization morphism is unramified away from \(t=0\), but is not unramified at the point lying over the cusp.



Relation to the cotangent space

Proposition 3 Let \(X\) be a scheme over \(k\) and \(x\in X\) be a closed point with residue field \(\kappa (x)\) separable over \(k\). Then the cotangent space of \(X\) at \(x\) is isomorphic to \(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\).


Proof. Apply the conormal sequence to the closed immersion \(\operatorname{Spec}(k(x))\hookrightarrow X\), we have a map \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\), where \(\mathfrak m_x\) is the maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\). We will show this surjection is actually a bijection. For convenience, let \(A=\mathcal O_{X,x}\) ,\(k'=\kappa(x)\) and \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_x\). Since the module of differentials is compatible with localization, it suffices to show that the map \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{A/k}\otimes k'\) is a bijection. By Yoneda lemma, it suffices to show that for any \(k'\)-module \(M\), the map \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\Omega_{A/k}\otimes k', M)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2, M)
\]
is a bijection. By the universal property of \(\Omega_{A/k}\), we have a bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}_{A}(\Omega_{A/k}, M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)\). By Lemma 2, we have \(\operatorname{Der}_k(k',M)=0\), which means that \[\operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)=\operatorname{Der}_{k'}(A,M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2,M).\]
One checks that this is just the map defined above, and the last isomorphism will be shown when we discuss formally étale.







TipVariety case



In case when \(X\) and \(Y\) are varieties and \(x\) is a \(k\)-point, by Lemma 1, we could deduce that \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2\) and \(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes k\) both come from the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. So they are isomorphic.

title: The Sheaf of Differentials and Unramified Morphisms
text:
Unramified morphisms

Definition 2 (unramified morphism) A morphism \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is unramified if it is locally of finite type and \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\).

By the transitivity sequence, unramified morphisms are stable under composition. By the base change property, unramified morphisms are stable under base change. One checks that unramified morphisms are also local on the target, so they are ``reasonable’’ in the sense of the textbook the rising sea.

Proposition 4 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism locally of finite type, then the locus in \(X\) where \(\pi\) is unramified is open.


Proof. The locus is the complement of \(\operatorname {supp}(\Omega_{X/Y})\), which is naturally open.


Examples
By the above calculation of \(\Omega_{A/B}\), we have the following corollaries.

Corollary 1 If \(L/K\) is a field extension of finite type, then \(\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is unramified if and only if \(L/K\) is a finite separable extension.


Proof. By Lemma 2, it suffices to show that if \(\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is unramified then \(L/K\) is a finite separable extension.
If \(L/K\) is inseparable, then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\) by the transitive exact sequence and Lemma 3. Thus, \(L/K\) is separable. If \(L/K\) is trancendental, then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\) by Lemma 4. Therefore, the extension \(L/K\) must be algebraic separable, which impies that \(L/K\) is finite since it is algebraic and of finite type.


Example 3 (coincidence in number theory) Let \(\phi:(A,\mathfrak m)\to (B,\mathfrak n)\) is a local morphism of finite type between local rings. Then \(\phi\) is unramifed if and only if \(B/\phi(\mathfrak m)B\) is a finite separable extension of \(A/\mathfrak m\).


Proof. It is a immediate consequence of Proposition 6.



Criterions of unramifiedness

Proposition 5 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) and \(\rho:Y\to Z\) be morphisms locally of finite type, and let \(\tau=\rho\circ\pi\). If \(\tau\) is unramified, then \(\pi\) is unramified.


Proof. The transitivity sequence gives a surjection \[
\Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow
\Omega_{X/Y}\longrightarrow 0.
\] Since \(\tau:X\to Z\) is unramified, we have \(\Omega_{X/Z}=0\). Therefore \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). As \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, it follows that \(\pi\) is unramified.


Proposition 6 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism locally of finite type. Then the following are equivalent.

\(\pi\) is unramifed,
for each point \(y\in Y\), \(\pi^{-1}(y)\) is the disjoint union of schemes of the form \(\operatorname {Spec} K\) where \(K\) is a finite separable extension of \(\kappa(y)\), and
for each geometric point \(\bar y\in Y\), \(\pi^{-1}(\bar y)\) is the disjoint union of copies of \(\bar y\).



Proof. Assersion 1 implies 2 and 3 by Corollary 1 and base change. Assersion 2 (resp. 3) implies that \(\Omega_{X/Y}|_y=0\) (resp. \(\Omega_{X/Y}|_{\bar y}=0\)). Since \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is of finte type, assersion 1 follows from the fact that if a quasicoherent sheaf \(\mathcal F\) of finite type on \(Y\) and \(\mathcal F|_y=0\) for all \(y\in Y\), then \(\mathcal F=0\). Note that \(\mathcal F|_y=0\) implies that \(\mathcal F_y=0\) by Nakayama’s lemma.


Proposition 7 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism between finite type schemes over an algebraically closed field \(k\). Then \(\pi\) is unramified if and only if \(\pi\) is injective on tangent vectors at closed points.


Proof. For any closed point \(x\in X\), let \(y\) be its image in \(Y\), then \(y\) is also a closed point \(Y\). By the transitive sequence, we have \[
\pi^*\Omega_{Y/k}\to\Omega_{X/k}\to\Omega_{X/Y}\to 0.
\]
Pullback to \(x=\operatorname{Spec}k\), we have \[
\Omega_{Y/k}|_y\to\Omega_{X/k}|_x\to\Omega_{X/Y}|_x\to 0.
\]
By Proposition 3 and the assumption, we know that \(\Omega_{Y/k}|_y\to\Omega_{X/k}|_x\) is the morphism between the corresponding cotangent spaces and hence surjective. Therfore, \(\Omega_{X/Y}|_x=0\), which mimplies that \(\pi\) is unramified at \(x\). Since the closed points are dense in \(X\), \(\pi\) is unramifed by Proposition 4.


Proposition 8 Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) be a morphism locally of finite type. Then \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is unramified if and only if its diagonal morphism \(X\to X\times_Y X\) is an open immersion.


Proof. We need a lemma. Let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow W\) be a closed immersion whose ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\) is of finite type. Then \(\mathcal I=\mathcal I^2\) if and only if \(i\) is also an open immersion.
Indeed, it is enough to work on an affine open subset \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq W\). Let \(I\subseteq A\) be the corresponding finitely generated ideal. Suppose that \(i\) is also an open immersion. Then we know that there exists an idempotent \(e\in A\) such that \[
A=Ae\oplus A(1-e)\text{ and }V(I)=V(e)=D(1-e).
\] Thus, the map \(A\to A/I\) equals to \(A\to A_{1-e}\), which implies that \(I=(e)\) and hence \(I=I^2\). Conversely, suppose \(I=I^2\), we will show that \(A\to A/I\) corresponds to an open immersion. Since \(I\) is finitely generated, there exists \(e\in I\) such that \((1-e)I=0\) by the proof of Nakayama’s lemma. Thus, \(e\) is an idempotent and \((e)\subseteq I\). Since \(x=ex\in (e)\) for any \(x\in I\), \(I=(e)\). Therefore, the map \(A\to A/I\) equals to \(A\to A_{1-e}\) corresponding to an open immersion.
We now apply the lemma to the diagonal. Since \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, \(\Delta_\pi\) is locally of finite presentation. To see this locally, write \[
B\longrightarrow A=B[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J.
\] The multiplication map \(A\otimes_BA\longrightarrow A\) has kernel generated by the finitely many elements \[
x_i\otimes1-1\otimes x_i,\qquad 1\leq i\leq n.
\] Thus the diagonal is, locally on its source and target, a closed immersion defined by an ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I\) of finite type.
Suppose first that \(\pi\) is unramified. Then \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). Since \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2\cong\Omega_{X/Y}\), it follows that \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2=0\), and hence \(\mathcal I=\mathcal I^2\). The lemma therefore shows, locally around every point of \(\Delta_\pi(X)\), that the diagonal is an open immersion. Hence \(\Delta_\pi\) is an open immersion.
Conversely, suppose that \(\Delta_\pi\) is an open immersion. An open immersion has zero conormal sheaf, so \(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2=0\), which implies that \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). Since \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, this is precisely the condition that \(\pi\) be unramified.







Caution



The condition that \(V(I)\hookrightarrow \operatorname{Spec} A\) is an open immersion is stronger than \(V(I)\) is open. For example, let \(A=k[x]/(x^2)\) and \(I=(x)\).



Corollary 2 Let \(\mathcal P\) be a class of morphisms stable under base change and restriction to open subschemes of the source. Let \(\pi:X\to Y\) and \(\rho:Y\to Z\) be morphisms, and set \(\tau=\rho\circ\pi\). If \(\rho\) is unramified and \(\tau\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\), then \(\pi\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\).
In particular, if \(\tau\) is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) (resp. étale), then so is \(\pi\).


Proof. Factor \(\pi\) as \[
X\xrightarrow{\Gamma_\pi}X\times_ZY
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{pr}_2}Y,
\qquad
\Gamma_\pi=(\operatorname{id}_X,\pi).
\] The square \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X & \xrightarrow{\Gamma_\pi} & X\times_ZY\\
{\scriptstyle\pi}\downarrow &&
\downarrow{\scriptstyle(\pi\circ\operatorname{pr}_1,\operatorname{pr}_2)}\\
Y & \xrightarrow{\Delta_\rho} & Y\times_ZY
\end{array}
\] is Cartesian. Since \(\rho\) is unramified, \(\Delta_\rho\) is an open immersion, and hence so is \(\Gamma_\pi\).
Moreover, \(\operatorname{pr}_2\) is the base change of \(\tau\) along \(\rho\), so it belongs to \(\mathcal P\). Thus \(\pi=\operatorname{pr}_2\circ\Gamma_\pi\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\) by stability under restriction to open subschemes of the source.


Proposition 9 Let \(\pi:X\to S\) be a morphism. Then \(\pi\) is unramified if and only if for every \(x\in X\) there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) and a locally closed immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow \mathbb A_S^n\) such that, if \(\mathcal J\) is the ideal sheaf defining \(j(U)\), then the differentials \(dg\), \(g\in\mathcal J\), generate \(\Omega^1_{\mathbb A_S^n/S}\) at \(j(x)\).


Proof. Assume first that \(\pi\) is unramified. Since \(\pi\) is locally of finite type, after shrinking around \(x\) and \(\pi(x)\) we may write \[
U=\operatorname{Spec}(A),\qquad
V=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\subset S,
\] with \(A\) a finitely generated \(B\)-algebra and \(U\) is the open neighborhood of \(x\). Choose a presentation \(A=B[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/I\). This gives a locally closed immersion \[
j:U\hookrightarrow \mathbb A_V^n\hookrightarrow \mathbb A_S^n.
\] The conormal sequence is \[
I/I^2
\xrightarrow{d}
\Omega^1_{B[T_1,\ldots,T_n]/B}\otimes_{B[T_1,\ldots,T_n]}A
\rightarrow
\Omega^1_{U/V}
\rightarrow 0.
\] Since \(\Omega_{X/S}=0\), we have \(\Omega^1_{U/V}=0\), so the first map is surjective. Hence the differentials \(dg\), \(g\in\mathcal J\), generate \(\Omega^1_{\mathbb A_S^n/S}\) at \(j(x)\).
Conversely, suppose the condition holds at every \(x\in X\). For such a locally closed immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb A_S^n\) with ideal sheaf \(\mathcal J\), the conormal sequence gives \[
\mathcal J/\mathcal J^2
\xrightarrow{d}
j^*\Omega^1_{\mathbb A_V^n/V}
\longrightarrow
\Omega^1_{U/V}
\longrightarrow 0
\] where \(V\) is an open of \(S\) such that \(j:U\to V\) is a closed immersion. Condition says that the first map is surjective at \(x\). Therefore \((\Omega^1_{U/S})_x=0\). Since this holds for every \(x\in X\), we conclude that \(\Omega_{X/S}\) equals to \(0\). Thus, \(\pi\) is unramified.

::: {def-formally-unramified name=“formally unramified”} A morphism of schemes \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is formally unramified if, for every affine scheme \(T\) over \(Y\) and every closed subscheme \(T_0\hookrightarrow T\) defined by a square-zero ideal sheaf, the natural map \[
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(T,X)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_Y(T_0,X)
\] is injective. :::
::: {prp-formally-unramified name=“formally unramified”} A morphism of schemes \(\pi\colon X\to Y\) is formally unramified if and only if \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\). :::

Proof. Since both conditions are local on the source and the target, we may assume \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\).
Suppose first that \(B\to A\) is formally unramified. Let \(I=\ker(A\otimes_B A\to A)\). Then \(\Omega_{A/B}\simeq I/I^2\). The morphism \((A\otimes_B A)/I^2\twoheadrightarrow A\) has square-zero kernel \(I/I^2\). Hence formal unramifiedness gives an injection \[
\operatorname{Hom}_B\bigl(A,(A\otimes_B A)/I^2\bigr)
\hookrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_B(A,A).
\] Consider the two morphisms \(\iota_1,\iota_2\colon A\to(A\otimes_B A)/I^2\) defined by \(\iota_1(r)=r\otimes1\) and \(\iota_2(r)=1\otimes r\). Their composites with the multiplication map to \(A\) coincide, so \(\iota_1=\iota_2\). Hence \(r\otimes1-1\otimes r\in I^2\) for every \(r\in A\). Since \(I/I^2\) is generated by the elements \(r\otimes1-1\otimes r\), we obtain \(I/I^2=0\). Therefore \(\Omega_{A/B}=0\).
Conversely, suppose that \(\Omega_{A/B}=0\). Let \(C\) be a \(B\)-algebra and let \(J\subset C\) be an ideal with \(J^2=0\). Suppose that \(\varphi,\psi\colon A\to C\) are two \(B\)-algebra morphisms whose composites with \(C\to C/J\) coincide.
Since \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) agree modulo \(J\), the map \[
d\colon A\to J,\qquad d(a)=\varphi(a)-\psi(a),
\] takes values in \(J\). Moreover, \(J\) acquires an \(A\)-module structure through either \(\varphi\) or \(\psi\); these two structures agree because \(J^2=0\). For \(a,b\in A\), we have \[
d(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)-\psi(a)\psi(b)=\varphi(a)d(b)+\psi(b)d(a)=a\,d(b)+b\,d(a).
\]
Thus \(d\) is a \(B\)-derivation. By the universal property of the sheaf of differentials, \[
\operatorname{Der}_B(A,J)
\simeq
\operatorname{Hom}_A(\Omega_{A/B},J)
=0.
\] Hence \(d=0\), so \(\varphi=\psi\). Therefore \(B\to A\) is formally unramified.
